How long does `map_structures()` take, and how much memory does it need, for a
dataset of a given shape and size? And the whole WB template pipeline, from
reading the CSV to validating the output? This page answers both for the latest
release. Each benchmark ran on a GitHub-hosted runner when the release was cut,
and re-measured earlier releases in the same run on the same machine, so the
comparison is like for like.

<!-- RESULTS -->

## WB template pipeline

The pipeline the notebook runs: read the CSV, keep the requested series, build
the structure map from the mapping workbook, `map_structures`,
`standardize_output`, `validate_dataset_local`. It is measured on a mock of the
World Bank's International Debt Statistics bronze extract, generated at the
sizes below from a profile of the real 147M-row file, in two configurations:
*whole frame*, the notebook's run with every column loaded, and *chunked, lean
load*, the production loop of the "Large files" guide, which reads the file in
five chunks without `Series_Name`, with the code columns as `category`, and
validates with `DatasetValidator`.

<!-- PIPELINE-RESULTS -->

## How it is measured

### `map_structures`

- **Four dataset shapes**, each generated with a fixed seed at 1,000 to
  1,000,000 rows (`benchmarks/scenarios.py` in the repository):
  - *typical*: an indicator table with six low-cardinality dimensions, mapped by
    three value maps, two implicit maps, two fixed values and one two-to-one
    multi-component map;
  - *high cardinality*: one column whose distinct values number a tenth of the
    rows, mapped through a 10,000-entry value map with a catch-all;
  - *regex heavy*: two columns where half the values miss the literal lookup and
    fall through to twenty regular expressions and a catch-all;
  - *wide*: twenty mapped columns.
- **Time** is the median of up to 7 calls (3 at 1,000,000 rows, and just one
  when a call takes over 30 seconds), measured with `time.perf_counter` after a
  warm-up call.
- **Peak extra memory** is the most memory one call allocated beyond its
  inputs, output included, measured with `tracemalloc` in a separate call.
  - It counts NumPy buffers, pandas hash tables and Python objects.
  - It misses memory allocated outside Python's allocator hooks, so these
    environments deliberately lack pyarrow: with it, pandas 3 keeps strings in
    Arrow buffers that `tracemalloc` cannot see.
  - A job's peak is roughly the input plus this figure.

### The pipeline

- **One mock dataset** (`benchmarks/wb_ids/` in the repository), rebuilt from
  the real file's profile with a fixed seed at each size, so every version
  reads the same bytes. Its shape, and how closely it tracks the real data, are
  described in `docs/datasets/wb-ids.md`.
- **Two configurations**: whole frame, and chunks of a fifth of the rows with
  the lean load. The chunked configuration needs `DatasetValidator`, so
  releases without it show "—" there.
- **Time** per step is the median over 3 runs (1 at more than 1,000,000 rows,
  and just one when a run takes over 30 seconds), as `benchmarks/wb_ids/pipeline.py`
  measures it: each step's own time, with the previous step's output already in
  memory.
- **Peak RSS** is the process's resident set size, sampled every 10 ms during
  the first run. It is what the operating system charges the job for: NumPy
  and Arrow buffers, Python objects and the allocator's caches alike, which is
  why these environments do carry pyarrow, as a Databricks cluster does. A
  spike shorter than 10 ms can be missed, and the figure includes the mock
  frame itself.
- **Like for like, twice.** The standardised output is fingerprinted chunk by
  chunk (its values, not their dtypes or order), and the validation errors are
  fingerprinted separately. A version whose output differs reads "≠ output"
  throughout; one whose validation found different errors reads it on the
  `validate` row alone.

### Both

- **Each version is installed as users install it**, with the dependencies it
  declares, resolved when the benchmark ran.
  - Versions that require different pandas releases are measured with different
    pandas releases, so part of a difference between them can come from pandas.
  - The Environment tables list what each version ran with.
- **Noise.** Runs on shared hardware vary by a few percent, so changes within
  ±10% read "≈ same". Versions whose code is unchanged differ by noise alone.
- **Cells marked "—" were not measured**, because a smaller size took over a
  minute, the run would not have fit in the machine's memory, the call failed,
  or (for `map_structures`) the call was too slow to trace its memory. The
  notes under each pipeline table, and the run's JSON, say which.
